variants.title: M275 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The M275 family covers several raw sub-codes that share the same core 90-degree V12 twin-turbo architecture but differ by displacement, output calibration, and application (standard flagship vs. AMG/Maybach). Identifying your exact sub-code is critical, as components like the ECU, turbo plumbing, and engine mounts are not universally interchangeable. #### M275.950 - 5.5L V12 Twin-Turbo (368kW / 500hp), 2002-2006 - **Fitted to:** Mercedes S-Class (W220 Facelift S 600), CL-Class (C215 Facelift) - **Key technical difference:** The initial 5.5-litre iteration of the M275, featuring port fuel injection and a specific early-generation engine management calibration. - **Sub-code-specific failure note:** Shares the family turbo wastegate rattle pattern; early turbo actuators are particularly prone to wear. - **Interchange note:** Not a straight swap with the 6.0L variants; the ECU, wiring loom, and exhaust manifolds differ significantly. #### M275.960 - 5.5L / 6.0L V12 Twin-Turbo (380kW-450kW), 2005-2013 - **Fitted to:** Mercedes S-Class (W221 S 600/S 65), CL-Class (C216) , SL-Class (R230) - **Key technical difference:** The most widely produced M275 variant, featuring updated turbochargers, revised cooling pathways, and in later W221 models, a transition to direct injection (CGI) in some markets, though primarily port-injected in the UK. - **Sub-code-specific failure note:** Shares the family pattern; HPFP wear becomes a more prominent consideration on higher-mileage W221 examples. - **Interchange note:** Requires the correct variant-specific engine mounts and transmission bell housing alignment; not universally interchangeable between S-Class and SL-Class without bracket modifications. #### M275.980 - 6.0L V12 Twin-Turbo (463kW / 630hp), 2002-2017 - **Fitted to:** Maybach (W240) , S 65 AMG (W221/W222), CL 65 AMG (C216) - **Key technical difference:** The high-output AMG and Maybach specification, featuring larger twin turbochargers, upgraded intercoolers, and a heavily reinforced bottom end to handle extreme torque loads. - **Sub-code-specific failure note:** Shares the family pattern, though the extreme thermal loads on AMG/Maybach applications can accelerate turbo bearing wear if oil change intervals are extended beyond 5,000 miles. - **Interchange note:** Completely incompatible with standard S600/CL600 applications due to different ECU architecture, turbo plumbing, and exhaust routing.

items.question: How much does a Mercedes M275 engine replacement cost in the UK?
items.answer: A Mercedes M275 engine replacement typically costs between £8,000 and £14,000 for a reconditioned supply-only unit . Fitted costs generally add £1,200-£1,600 for independent specialist labour due to V12 complexity, and fully rebuilt units with upgraded thermal management components can reach £12,000-£18,000 supply-only.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the Mercedes M275 engine?
items.answer: The most documented failure patterns for the M275 are turbocharger wastegate rattle/bearing wear and high-pressure fuel pump (HPFP) degradation. Early warning signs include a metallic rattle on deceleration, boost pressure faults, or rough idle and extended cranking times, and if turbo bearing wear leads to oil ingestion, or fuel dilution damages the crankshaft bearings, a full engine replacement is required.

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the M275 engine?
items.answer: The M275 is fitted to Mercedes-Benz flagship models from 2002 to 2017, including the S-Class (W220, W221, W222), CL-Class (C215, C216), SL-Class (R230), and Maybach (W240). It powers badges ranging from the S 600 and CL 600 to the S 65 AMG and Maybach 62, and you should always verify your exact sub-code via registration lookup before ordering parts.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Mercedes M275 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes M275 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the well-documented turbocharger and HPFP failure risks. Used units carry a high probability of inheriting the same latent thermal degradation or oil starvation damage unless accompanied by stamped proof of preventative turbo/HPFP replacement, whereas a proper reconditioned M275 includes new or upgraded twin turbochargers, refreshed HPFP components, and new valve cover gaskets as standard.

items.question: What is the difference between the M275.950, M275.960, and M275.980?
items.answer: The M275.950 is the early 5.5L variant, the M275.960 is the widely produced 5.5L/6.0L standard variant, and the M275.980 is the high-output 6.0L AMG and Maybach specification. While they share the same core 90-degree V12 twin-turbo architecture, they differ in displacement, turbo sizing, and ECU calibration, meaning fitting a .950 or .980 as a direct replacement for a .960 will result in severe ECU, wiring loom, and exhaust manifold incompatibilities.
